asDecan.p: Every sign is split into three ten-degree slices called decans, and each slice gets a planet of its own. Your Sun is somewhere in the first ten degrees of Gemini, the very start of the sign, where Gemini is at its freshest and most like itself, and the Golden Dawn hands that slice to Jupiter. It's an awkward fit, to be honest. Jupiter's home is Sagittarius, the sign opposite Gemini, so here it's in detriment, which means it has to work against the grain. Jupiter wants the big picture, one belief you can stand on. Gemini, ruled by Mercury, wants the next fact, the other side of the argument, the footnote. Drop Jupiter in there and it enlarges everything it finds, including the doubts. The Nine of Swords after you is Mars in Gemini, lying awake at three in the morning. The Ten belongs to the Sun, where it all finally stops. Yours is the first of the three, the woman standing among the swords with open ground behind her. The Lovers is still your Sun card, and this is the finer grain inside it.

You've got fourteen tabs open on your phone and at least three of them are about the same decision. Choosing a sofa, or a school for a kid, or a new phone plan, you'll read every review, ask four friends, and come back to the first option a fortnight later. At a family dinner you're the one who can argue any side, and you'll sometimes swap sides halfway through just to see if it holds up. A text from your boss saying 'can we have a quick chat tomorrow' can eat your whole evening, because by nine o'clock you've built five versions of what it might mean. You're also very good company on a long car trip. You know a little about almost everything, and people tend to come away from talking with you feeling livelier than when they arrived.

The less obvious gift is that you can see other people's cages very clearly. A friend says they can't possibly ask for flexible hours, and you're the one who asks whether anyone has actually said no or whether they've just assumed it. You'll read the tenancy agreement a mate is panicking about and find the clause that lets them out early. Jupiter struggles in Gemini, and I think that's partly why this works. You've had so much practice untangling your own knots that you've got quick at other people's. You're also good at the generous second opinion. When two people at work have fallen out, you can usually find the version of events where nobody's the villain, and saying it out loud tends to calm the whole office down.

Where it shows is your calendar. Jupiter is generous and Gemini says yes to anything interesting, so you agree to the book club, the side project, helping your cousin move, and the short course you found at midnight. Three weeks later you feel boxed in and a bit resentful, and it's hard to see that you built most of the box yourself, one yes at a time. There's a quieter one too. You can tell the story of being stuck so well, so funny and so detailed, that telling it starts to stand in for doing anything about it. Your friends have been hearing about the job you're about to leave for two years. They enjoy the story. That's a bit of a problem, because it means nobody ever pushes you.

When something goes wrong, a redundancy or a health scare in the family or a friend who's stopped speaking to you, your first move is to find out everything. You read, you ring people, you ask the same question three different ways. That helps for about two days. By the end of the week you've often gone still. The email's unanswered, the appointment isn't booked, and you're sleeping badly because your head keeps running the cases at night. The people around you tend to get either a long anxious commentary or silence, and both are hard to help with. What actually helps is shrinking it. Pick one question you can get a real answer to within a few days and go and get it. Walking helps too, oddly, as if moving your legs loosens your thinking.

The Lovers is a card about choosing, and this slice of Gemini finds choosing hard, which is a bit of a joke the chart plays on you. In love it usually shows up after the choice has been made. You're with someone, it's fine, it's good even, and some part of you keeps a quiet file of other lives you could be living. You don't act on it. You just leave the door ajar in your head, and a partner can feel that even when they can't name it. People with this Sun are often drawn to someone certain, a person with a big simple view of life who says 'we're doing this' and means it. That can be lovely, since it's the long view Jupiter can't quite hold in you. It can also mean you hand them the steering wheel and then quietly resent where they drive.

Gemini gives you range and Jupiter gives you appetite, so you're good wherever breadth is the job. Journalism, research, teaching, sales, policy, recruitment, any customer-facing role where every day brings a different problem, anything that pays you to learn quickly and explain it well. The snag tends to be in the fine print of your own situation. I've seen a lot of people in this part of Gemini assume there's a rule stopping them from moving sideways, asking for training or changing teams, and never check. Ask HR the actual question. Ask your manager. Surprisingly often the answer is yes and nobody thought to say so. You also do well alongside one colleague who's good at finishing things, and if you've found that person, keep hold of them.

At twenty this part of Gemini is often dazzling and all over the place. Two degrees started, a band, three part-time jobs, and a lot of worry about picking the wrong life, which seems to be the main fear at that age. There's often a stretch in the twenties of feeling stuck while surrounded by options, which is a confusing thing to explain to anyone. By the mid-thirties most people with this Sun have worked out that putting off a choice is a choice too, and they start committing to fewer things and finding they lose less than they feared. The fifties tend to be kind to them. The worrying gets smaller, Jupiter's long view seems to arrive late, and a lot of them become the person everyone rings to talk something through.

Next time you feel boxed in by something, a job, a lease, a commitment you made in a weak moment, write the rule that's keeping you there on a scrap of paper in one plain sentence. 'I can't leave before the contract ends.' 'I have to go to every one of these.' Then find out, from the person or the document, whether that rule is real. Do it for one rule only. Sometimes it's softer than you thought and sometimes it isn't, and either way you're working with a fact.
